product.title: Gantry
product.description: A game-agnostic content framework. Experiences compose into a declared dependency tree and activate in observable stages, with game feature plugins reference counted across swaps, so shipped content and side-loaded mods travel the same path with load order computed instead of curated. Loads are tracked as named, tagged scopes, so a loading bar can say "Environment 12/40" and a live editor panel can attribute a hitch to the scope that caused it.

The extension mechanism for every pluggable Gantry class.

The problem this solves is specific and catches everyone once. Unreal instantiates a subsystem for **every** non-abstract subclass it finds. So the moment a game does:

```cpp
class UMyGameExperienceSubsystem : public UGantryExperienceSubsystem { ... };
```

the engine happily creates BOTH the Gantry base and the game's subclass, and now two runtimes are fighting over the same job. Marking the base abstract is not a fix either, because then a project that wants plain Gantry behaviour has nothing to instantiate.

The fix is that exactly one class in each hierarchy is "selected", named by a soft class path in the project's ini, and every other class in that hierarchy declines to be created:

```cpp
bool UGantryExperienceSubsystem::ShouldCreateSubsystem(UObject* Outer) const
{
 return GantryCore::IsSelectedClass(GetClass(), Settings->ExperienceSubsystemClass, StaticClass());
}
```

A game then writes one line in DefaultGame.ini, in the settings section of the module that owns the hierarchy:

```cpp
[/Script/GantryExperience.GantryExperienceSettings]
ExperienceSubsystemClass=/Script/MyGame.MyGameExperienceSubsystem
```

and its subclass is the only one created. Leave the setting empty and the Gantry default runs. Gantry's selectable hierarchies are the experience subsystem (ExperienceSubsystemClass, in the Gantry Experience settings) and the streaming subsystem (StreamingSubsystemClass, in the Gantry Gauge settings).

Result codes, status values and generational handles shared by every Gantry module.

This is the vocabulary the rest of Gantry speaks, so it is deliberately small and makes no assumptions: nothing here depends on a UWorld, and nothing presumes anything about the game using Gantry. Functions that can fail in more than one interesting way return an FGantryStatus; systems that hand out references into pooled storage hand out FGantryHandle.

Generational handle into a dense array.

A raw index into a pooled array goes stale silently: slot 7 is freed, slot 7 is reused, and the old index now addresses a live but wrong record. Bumping a serial on free makes the stale handle detectably invalid instead. The owner of the array validates a handle by comparing its serial with the slot's current one; the handle alone can only say whether it addresses a slot at all.

Serial is signed because UHT will not expose unsigned integers to Blueprint. It only increments, and would need billions of reuse cycles on one slot to reach the sign bit.

Engine feature switches shared by every Gantry module.

Gantry supports the three latest engine releases. The oldest is the floor every code path must compile against; newer engines light up better implementations where they exist. Each switch names the capability rather than the version, so call sites read as what they need and the version mapping lives in exactly one place. Each is 1 when the running engine has the capability and 0 otherwise, so test them with `#if`, never `#ifdef`.

Including this header on an engine older than the floor is a compile error that says so.

The GantryCore runtime module: shared vocabulary, class selection and tag validation.

Loads at PreDefault, before the game module, because the things it validates — class selections and tag requirements — are consulted during other systems' startup. It owns no runtime state: this module is a place for shared vocabulary, not a service.

GantryCore's log categories.

Raise or lower one channel at a time from the console, e.g. `Log LogGantryTags Verbose`, or persistently under [Core.Log] in DefaultEngine.ini. Each Gantry module declares its own channels, so a project can quieten one system without losing the others.

Settings shared by every Gantry module, under Project Settings -> Plugins -> Gantry Core.

Deliberately small. Each Gantry module owns the settings for its own concern (Gauge its ledger tunables, Experience its tree root), so nothing here belongs to a system a project might not use. Stored in DefaultGame.ini under [/Script/GantryCore.GantryCoreSettings].

The gameplay tags GantryCore declares natively, and Gantry's stance on tags.

Gantry's position on gameplay tags is deliberately narrow, because a framework that ships opinions about a game's taxonomy is a framework nobody can reuse:

- Gantry declares tags only for its own framework mechanics.
- Gantry never declares gameplay tags. No Damage.*, no Ability.*, no State.*. Those belong to the game, and a game that inherits somebody else's taxonomy has already lost.
- Games and downstream plugins register their own tag sources through GantryTagRegistry, so their tags live in their own ini and travel with their own plugin.

The practical value Gantry adds over raw gameplay tags is validation: a tag that a system *requires* can be declared as a requirement and checked once at startup, instead of silently resolving to an empty tag at the call site three hours into a session.

### Component bring-up stages

The four InitState tags below are the stages a modular gameplay component advances through, as the engine's UGameFrameworkComponentManager consumes them. They are unprefixed, unlike every other tag Gantry declares. These four strings are the vocabulary the engine's modular gameplay samples established, and any third-party component written against that convention expects them by name. Relocating them under Gantry.* would fork the vocabulary and quietly break every component that did not know to follow.

They are declared here so a project does not have to redeclare them. Gantry never advances an actor through the chain itself; driving the sequence is the game's job.

The sequence exists because actor initialisation cannot be ordered in advance: a pawn spawns, its player state replicates whenever the network delivers it, and its data assets finish loading at a third unrelated moment. Rather than guessing an order, each component advances as far as its own prerequisites allow and re-evaluates whenever anything else moves.

Registration and validation of tags a system depends on.

Gameplay tags trade compile-time safety for runtime extensibility: a tag referenced by name that nobody registered resolves to an empty FGameplayTag, and the code using it quietly does nothing. That failure surfaces hours later as "the ability doesn't fire" with no log line anywhere.

A requirement turns that into one startup error naming the tag and the system that wanted it. Register requirements during module startup, then call ValidateRequirements once tags are loaded.

```cpp
GantryTagRegistry::RequireTag(TEXT("MyGame.Ability.Dash"), TEXT("MyGame ability system"));
```

This is deliberately not a tag *source*. Sources are ini files and native declarations, owned by whoever owns the tags. Gantry only cares whether the tags it was promised actually exist.

GantryCore validates every registered requirement once the engine has initialised, and the Gantry.Core.ValidateTags console command re-runs the check on demand. Registration is thread-safe; validation and lookups need the gameplay tag manager, so run them on the game thread.

The GantryCoreEditor module: the editor chrome every Gantry editor module shares.

Owns the icon style set, the "Gantry" section of the editor's Tools menu, and the commands that belong to no particular system (open Gantry's settings, re-validate tags). The other Gantry editor modules add their own entries to the same named section through ToolMenus rather than depending on this module's internals, so every Gantry tool appears under one heading.

Slate style for Gantry's editor UI: the icons its toolbar, menu and tab entries use.

Content root is the plugin's Resources directory, so the plugin icon doubles as the toolbar, menu and tab icon rather than needing separate art. Other Gantry editor modules reference its brushes by style set name (GetStyleSetName) and brush name, e.g. "Gantry.Icon".

An inclusive version window, expressed as dotted numeric strings ("1.4.2").

Either end may be empty, meaning unbounded. Comparison is component-wise numeric rather than lexicographic, because "1.10.0" is newer than "1.9.0" and a string compare disagrees.

Provenance for one shipped unit of content, whether that unit is an experience or a plugin.

### Stamped versus authored

Engine version, game version and build number are facts about a cook, not decisions a designer makes. If they were editable somebody would eventually type the wrong one, and every compatibility check downstream would become theatre. They are VisibleAnywhere and written by Stamp() during save-for-cook; the authored half below is what a human actually decides.

### Mirrored into asset registry tags

Compatibility has to be answerable *before* committing to a load. A menu that greys out an incompatible entry cannot afford to load the thing first to find out. Owners of this struct override GetAssetRegistryTags and call AppendAssetRegistryTags so the registry can answer.

Game builds this content declares support for.

Checked as a range rather than for equality: content almost never breaks on the first patch after it ships, and equality would force a recook of every unit on every game version bump.

Free-form tags describing what this unit provides or needs.

Gantry never interprets these. They exist so a game can gate content on its own axes (platform, storefront, rating) without Gantry growing a field per axis. They are not mirrored into asset registry tags, so metadata rebuilt by FromAssetData has none.

The one root of a project's experience tree.

### A class instead of a flag

A project has exactly one base experience, and that fact is worth more as a type than as data. UGantryExperienceSettings::BaseExperience only accepts this class, so the root cannot be mispointed; there is no Kind enum to set wrong, and "which experience is the base" has one answer enforced by the compiler and the property editor rather than by validation prose.

### What it adds structurally

Nothing. Children, stages, optional dependencies all live on the common class, because any experience can own children — the base is distinguished by being the root, not by capability. The overrides below only pin down root-ness: depth zero, no parents, no attachments.

Its Children listing doubles as the project's content registry: the base ships in chunk 0, so its entries are readable even when the content they describe is not installed. That is what lets a menu draw "Experience C — not installed" about a pak that is not there.

Experience auto-activated when a world begins play and nothing else has set one. Optional.

Lives here rather than in project settings because it is a content decision: the root declares its tree, so it declares its starting leaf too. Any experience reachable from this base qualifies — a direct child or a deeper descendant; validation rejects anything the tree cannot reach, because an unreachable default is a boot into a guaranteed failure.

Cook-time snapshot of one listed child: everything showable about it without loading it.

Machine-written, never authored. The child's own definition is the single source of truth for its tag, name, description and metadata; these rows are copied from the loaded children during cook (RebuildChildSnapshots) so an *absent* experience stays describable — its pak unmounted, its definition unloadable, this snapshot the only place its name can come from. Regenerated on every cook, so it cannot drift.

A named composite of content, activated in stages.

Gantry's stance is that it should know how to *sequence* content, not what content is. So there is deliberately no pawn data here, no ability sets, no game mode. A game subclasses this and adds whatever its own systems need; Gantry runs the stages and the game reads its own properties from OnExperienceReady.

### The tree

Experiences form a tree rooted at the project's one UGantryBaseExperienceDefinition. Edges are authored by whoever has write access to author them:

- **Owners list children.** A shipped parent names what belongs under it in Children. Being listed is what makes an experience activatable: the chain from root to leaf is the required dependency chain, and activation flattens it root-first.
- **Wanters declare wants.** Any experience may name OptionalDependencies by tag. These never gate activation; when present they are pulled into the chain and ordered first, when absent they are skipped and the dependent is expected to cope (query IsExperienceActive and branch).
- **Side-loaded content attaches itself.** A mod cannot edit shipped assets, so it declares its required parent(s) in AttachTo. Shipped listed content leaves AttachTo empty; validation rejects an asset that is both listed and self-attaching.

The tree is crawled by FGantryExperienceTree (Discover -> Resolve -> Validate) before anything activates. An experience reachable by neither listing nor scan does not exist; one that is present but unresolvable is a visible orphan.

Machine identity: assigned once at asset creation, regenerated on duplication, never edited.

Three identities, three jobs. The asset *path* is where it lives and breaks on a move. The *tag* is the human identity — designer-authored, used by code and UI, and renameable when a taxonomy changes. The *guid* survives both, which is what save games, server verification, and mod databases need: a name for the content that no refactor can invalidate.

Free-form payload for the game.

Gantry never reads this. It exists so a project can attach its own data object without subclassing, which is often enough and keeps the asset type count down.

Experiences that belong under this one. Owner side of the tree.

Just the assets — everything about a child (tag, name, description, metadata) is authored on the child itself, which is the only place it makes sense to live. Each child may be listed by exactly one parent; a duplicate listing fails the tree crawl.

Soft on purpose: a listed child's content may not be mounted, and the listing must survive that. ChildSnapshots below is what keeps an absent child describable.

Cook-time copies of each child's display data, for when the child itself is absent.

Machine-written by RebuildChildSnapshots during cook, and deliberately absent from the details panel: there is no correct human interaction with a machine-maintained cache, so it offers none. Inspect it through the tree's availability queries, or a debugger.

Experiences this one wants but does not need. Wanter side; never gates activation.

A present optional dependency joins the activation chain and is ordered before this experience. An absent one is skipped, and it is this experience's responsibility to cope — query UGantryExperienceSubsystem::IsExperienceActive and branch.

Required parent(s), declared by side-loaded content that no shipped asset can list.

Shipped content leaves this empty and gets its parent from whoever lists it. Multiple entries are legal for side-loaded content only — the compatibility-patch pattern, "requires A and B" — and every named parent must resolve or this experience is an orphan.

One step of an experience activation.

Stages are instanced objects on the definition, so designers configure them per experience. Gantry runs them strictly in order and waits for each to report completion, which means a stage may be asynchronous without any of its neighbours caring.

Override BeginStage, call StartStage first, then FinishStage when done — immediately or frames later. The default implementation finishes at once, so a stage with no work needs no override. EndStage undoes the work and runs in reverse order on deactivation. Everything here runs on the game thread.

Stage that loads a list of assets before the experience is considered ready.

Everything goes through UGantryAssetManager, so the loading screen sees a named scope with real counts rather than a stall it cannot explain. The project's AssetManagerClassName must name UGantryAssetManager or a subclass; without it the stage fails.

Stage that loads and activates game feature plugins, reference counted across experiences.

This is the only stage that touches GameFeatures, which keeps the pipeline itself free of that dependency: an experience that activates no plugins never goes near the subsystem.

### Reference counting

Two experiences can legitimately want the same plugin. A shared plugin — props used by more than one experience, say — must survive a switch from one to the other, and the bare subsystem API has no way to know anyone else still wants it. So activation is always reference counted:

- 5.8+: through FGameFeatureStateHandleReferenceController. The handle owns this stage's references; releasing it downgrades only the plugins nobody else holds.
- 5.6 / 5.7: through Gantry's own process-wide counts, keyed by plugin URL. Same contract, minus the engine's dependency tracking: a plugin's dependencies stay up until the engine itself decides otherwise.

### Two completion signals

The plugin state machine reporting Active is not the same as the plugin being ready. Actions run during activation and the engine gives them no way to report async completion, so UGantryGameFeatureAction supplies that separately. This stage waits on both: the batch load callback, and then the action tracker draining. Waiting on only the first is why a loading screen disappears while the world is still assembling itself.

Release this stage's plugin references when the experience ends.

Release, not deactivate: a plugin another experience still holds stays up. Turning this off leaks references for the lifetime of the process and is only ever right for a plugin that must outlive every experience.

World subsystem that activates, runs and tears down one experience per game or PIE world.

The pipeline is intentionally dull: resolve the definition, flatten its stages, run them in order, report each into the load ledger, then announce readiness. Nothing here knows what the stages actually do, which is what lets a game add its own without touching Gantry. Its API is game thread only.

### Scoped to a world

An experience is scoped to a world: travel to a new map and the old experience is gone. Anything that must outlive that belongs on an engine or game instance subsystem instead.

### Extending

A game subclasses this and names the subclass in DefaultGame.ini (or in Project Settings -> Plugins -> Gantry Experience):

```cpp
[/Script/GantryExperience.GantryExperienceSettings]
ExperienceSubsystemClass=/Script/MyGame.MyGameExperienceSubsystem
```

ShouldCreateSubsystem then declines for every class except the selected one. Without that, Unreal instantiates both this and the subclass and they fight over the same world.

Activates an experience by identity, replacing any current one.

The tag is resolved through the crawled tree: the leaf's required chain plus its present optional dependencies, ordered shallow to deep. An experience the tree does not know cannot activate — being listed (or being side-loaded content whose attachment resolves) is what makes activation possible. Asynchronous; listen on OnExperienceReady.

Ignored, with a warning, while another activation is still Resolving or Loading. An unresolvable chain sets the state to Failed. The outgoing experience's stages are stood down only once the incoming one is ready, so anything both hold stays up across the swap.

@param ExperienceTag Identity tag of the leaf experience to activate. Empty is ignored.

Discards the crawled tree so the next activation re-crawls.

Call after mounting or unmounting content mid-session. Deliberately does not touch a live chain: newly mounted content participates at the next activation, never by hot-grafting into a running experience.

Runs a callback once the experience is ready, immediately if it already is.

This is the accessor game code should use. Binding OnExperienceReady directly races: if the experience finished before you bound, your callback never fires.

### Priority tiers

Three tiers, fired high to low, so a system can be sure the things it depends on are already standing. The usual split: subsystems that set up for gameplay bind high, ordinary gameplay systems bind normal, and anything reacting to a fully assembled world binds low.

Tiers are not stages. A stage runs *during* load and is authored per experience in the data asset; a tier fires *after* ready and is bound by code at runtime. Game code cannot add a stage — stages are instanced objects on the definition — so anything wanting "run me once the experience is up" is a tier.

This entry point registers on the high tier, fired first.

Ends the stages of the experience being replaced.

Deferred until the incoming experience is standing, so that anything both experiences hold — a shared game feature plugin, most obviously — never drops to zero references and churns through a teardown and rebuild in between.

One known experience, however it became known.

A node exists if the experience is *listed* (named by an installed ancestor's Children entry) or *present* (its definition asset was found and loaded). Listed-but-absent nodes carry only their entry's display metadata; that is the point of carrying it.

The crawled experience tree: every experience the game knows about and how they relate.

### Discover -> Resolve -> Validate

Build runs three phases:

- **Discover.** Walk the base's Children listings recursively (knows everything *listed*, even uninstalled), then scan the asset registry for experience definitions nothing listed (knows everything *present*, even unlisted — side-loaded content). Union of both is the known universe. Discovery only reads; nothing here activates anything.
- **Resolve.** Connect edges. Listed children get their lister as required parent; scanned content gets its AttachTo tags. An attachment naming a tag nobody has is an orphan — visible, present, MissingDependency.
- **Validate.** Cycle-check the combined graph (required plus known-optional edges — an optional cycle is still an authoring error, because "optional" means may-be-absent, not may-be-unordered), then compute depth by longest-path layering and settle availability.

### Ordering

Depth is longest path from the root over the combined graph, which makes shallow-to-deep a provably valid topological order: every dependency is strictly shallower than its dependent by construction. Ties break by tag, so the order is identical on every machine — a requirement, not a nicety, the moment two players need matching content states. Activation runs shallow to deep; teardown unwinds deep to shallow.

Build is synchronous and loads every reachable definition. They are small data assets and the stage list must be known before any pipeline starts. The tree is a plain value owned by its caller and is not thread-safe; build and query it on the game thread.

Crawls from the given root, replacing anything built before. Returns false on a structural fault — cycle, duplicate listing, listed-and-attached ambiguity — with OutError naming it. Per-node problems (absent content, incompatibility, orphaned attachments) are not faults; they land in node availability. Loads every reachable definition synchronously.

Assembles the activation chain for a leaf: its required closure, plus every *present* optional dependency of that closure (with their own required closures), ordered shallow to deep with ties broken by tag. Returns false if the leaf is unknown or anything in the required closure is not Available; absent optionals are skipped without comment beyond a verbose log — coping with their absence is the dependent's declared responsibility.

Shared vocabulary of the experience framework: availability, lifecycle state, and the events that report them.

An experience is "a named composite of content that gets loaded and switched on in stages." That is all Gantry commits to. It deliberately does not know what the content *is* — no pawn data, no ability sets, no game mode assumptions. Those belong to the game, and a framework that bakes them in is a framework that only works for the game it was extracted from.

The pipeline is a list of stages run in order. Each stage reports into the load ledger, so the loading screen gets staged, named progress instead of one boolean at the end. Gantry ships the stages it can implement generically (asset loading, game feature activation); a game adds its own by subclassing UGantryExperienceStage.

Whether an experience can be played right now, and if not, why not.

Visibility and activatability are separate questions with separate mechanisms. An experience is *visible* if it is either present (found by the registry scan) or listed (named by an installed ancestor's entry). It is *activatable* only if its whole required chain resolves. The states below are the four ways those two answers combine.

Process-wide accounting for game feature actions that are still working.

### Why it exists

There is an asymmetry in the engine. Deactivation can be asynchronous — FGameFeatureDeactivatingContext::PauseDeactivationUntilComplete hands you a delegate to call when you are done. Activation cannot: FGameFeatureActivatingContext carries no such mechanism. So an action that loads something on activation has no way to say "not finished yet", and the plugin reports Active while the action is still working.

That is precisely the blind spot the load ledger exists to eliminate. This tracker is the missing signal: actions declare outstanding work, and UGantryExperienceStage_GameFeatures waits on it in addition to the plugin state machine's own completion.

### Known limitation

The count is global, not per world context. Actions apply per context — see FGameFeatureStateChangeContext::ShouldApplyToWorldContext — so under PIE with several clients, one client's outstanding actions will hold another client's stage open. It is conservative rather than wrong: the stage waits too long, never too little.

Game thread only; the count is not synchronised.

Base class for game feature actions that Gantry can see.

Gantry ships this and nothing derived from it. AddComponents, AddAbilities, AddWidgets and their kin are all game-shaped, and a framework that ships them is a framework built for one game.

The value here is the async contract the engine does not provide. Override BeginActivation instead of OnGameFeatureActivating, and call FinishActivation when the work is genuinely done — which may be several frames later:

```cpp
void UMyAction::BeginActivation(const FGameFeatureActivatingContext& Context)
{
 Manager->RequestAsyncLoad(Paths, FStreamableDelegate::CreateUObject(
 this, &UMyAction::HandleLoaded));
}
```

```cpp
void UMyAction::HandleLoaded() { FinishActivation(); }
```

A synchronous action overrides nothing extra; the default BeginActivation finishes at once. This mirrors UGantryExperienceStage's BeginStage/FinishStage, so there is one idiom for "override Begin, call Finish, async is free" across the whole plugin.

Game feature data carrying Gantry's shipped-unit provenance.

### Plugin metadata and experience metadata

A plugin is the unit that actually ships: one cook, one pak, one set of binaries. Engine version and game version are facts about that cook, so repeating them on every experience inside the plugin would be ten copies of one truth, nine of which can drift.

An experience still carries its own metadata, because an experience in chunk 0 ships with the base game and has no plugin to inherit from. Where both exist, the plugin's is authoritative for mounting and the experience's for selection.

### Use

Set this as the GameFeatureData class for a plugin by choosing it when creating the plugin's data asset, or by pointing an existing asset's class at it. A plugin that does this takes a dependency on the Gantry plugin's GantryExperience module, which is worth entering deliberately: once plugins ship against it, Gantry cannot be lifted out of the project.

Gantry's game feature policy, and the single place compatibility is enforced.

### One gate

IsPluginAllowed is consulted before a plugin is mounted, and it can refuse with a reason string. Every other candidate location — the experience stage, the catalog, a menu — is downstream of a decision already taken, and putting the check there means writing it several times and having the copies disagree. One gate, consulted by everything.

### Enable it

```cpp
[/Script/GameFeatures.GameFeaturesSubsystemSettings]
GameFeaturesManagerClassName=/Script/GantryExperience.GantryGameFeaturesProjectPolicies
```

That line goes in DefaultGame.ini. Derives from UDefaultGameFeaturesProjectPolicies rather than the abstract base, so everything not overridden keeps engine-default behaviour.

Checks a plugin's shipped-unit metadata without mounting it.

Reads the asset registry tags written by UGantryGameFeatureData, so this is answerable for a plugin that is merely known rather than installed. A plugin with no Gantry metadata is allowed: plenty of legitimate plugins do not use Gantry, and refusing them would be a policy about their authorship rather than their compatibility. Unstamped metadata is treated as compatible too.

Refuse plugins whose metadata does not match this build.

Exposed as a switch because during development the answer is often "let it through and warn", whereas a shipped build wants the refusal. Defaults to enforcing.

Runtime module for Gantry's experience framework: definitions, the tree crawl, stages and activation.

Loads at PreDefault so its settings and primary asset types are registered before the asset manager scans. It owns no runtime state; the experience tree is built on demand by the world subsystem and discarded with it.

Project-wide Gantry Experience configuration, under Project Settings -> Plugins -> Gantry Experience, saved to DefaultGame.ini.

Deliberately thin. Almost everything about a project's experiences is a *content* decision and lives on the base experience asset — which experiences exist, which one starts, how they compose. Engine config only needs to know where the root is.

The root of the project's experience tree, and its registry of record.

Typed to UGantryBaseExperienceDefinition so the root cannot be mispointed — the type system is the enforcement, not validation prose. Designated by path, never found by name, because a search would eventually find Base_OLD in a shipped build. Empty means the project does not use experiences, and worlds start without one.

Its Children listing is what the tree crawl walks; ship it in chunk 0 so the listing stays readable when the content it describes is not installed.

Native gameplay tags naming the steps of an experience activation.

Pipeline mechanics only — which step of an activation is running — so progress can be reported and filtered by stage. Identity tags for the experiences themselves belong to the game; see the Categories metadata on UGantryExperienceDefinition::ExperienceTag for how a project narrows the picker to its own root.

Asset manager through which every Gantry load is requested, so each one is recorded as a named scope in the load ledger.

Wired up via [/Script/Engine.Engine] AssetManagerClassName= in DefaultEngine.ini. It is created before the game instance, which makes it the earliest place the project owns.

Its job is not to be clever about loading; FStreamableManager is already good at that. Its job is to make every request **named and attributed**, so the ledger can report "Environment 12/40" instead of an anonymous percentage. Every entry point here opens a scope, attaches the handle, and closes on completion.

A game that wants its own asset manager subclasses this and sets AssetManagerClassName to the subclass. Because the engine resolves that by name rather than by scanning subclasses, this hierarchy does not need the class-selection dance the subsystems use.

Runtime module that owns the process-wide load ledger and the Gantry Gauge console commands.

Loads at PreDefault, before the game module and before the asset manager exists, which is why it owns the load ledger. The ledger has to be able to record the primary asset scan, and that happens before any subsystem is alive.

Ownership summary:

- FGantryGaugeModule owns the ledger (module lifetime).
- UGantryStreamingSubsystem ticks it and publishes it (engine lifetime).
- UGantryAssetManager feeds it (engine lifetime).

The broker every Gantry load request passes through, and the record of what happened.

Deliberately not a UObject. It is created before the engine has a game instance, it is touched from async loading callbacks on arbitrary threads, and it must never be a GC consideration. There is one ledger per process, owned by FGantryGaugeModule and reached through FGantryGaugeModule::GetLedger.

### The one rule

The ledger is only truthful if it is the only door. Code that calls LoadSynchronous or holds a hard UPROPERTY reference is invisible to it, and a loading bar with blind spots is worse than no loading bar because it reports "done" while the game is still hitching. Route requests through UGantryAssetManager, and use FGantryLoadSnapshot::EngineAsyncPackageCount to catch the leaks.

### Threading

The recording calls (OpenScope, AttachHandle, AddManualWork, CompleteManualWork, CloseScope) may be called from any thread and take a short lock. OpenScope and CloseScope broadcast their event on the calling thread, after releasing the lock. Poll is expected on the game thread and is the only source of OnScopeProgress. Readers never see a live record; they get a value-type snapshot copied under one lock.

RAII wrapper that opens a load scope on construction and closes it when it leaves scope.

For synchronous or early-return-heavy code where an explicit CloseScope is easy to miss:

```cpp
FGantryLoadScopeGuard Guard(TEXT("Bootstrap"), GantryGaugeTags::Load_Scope_Bootstrap);
if (Failed()) { Guard.Fail(); return; } // still closed, marked Failed
```

For async work the scope outlives the stack frame, so use the ledger directly and close from the completion delegate instead, or hand the scope over with Release.

Blueprint access to the loading value types.

UFUNCTION cannot appear inside a USTRUCT, so the accessors on FGantryLoadScopeInfo and FGantryLoadSnapshot are plain C++ and surface to Blueprint here. Keeping them as struct methods as well means C++ callers do not have to route through a library.

Value types that describe asset loading as named, tagged scopes rather than individual assets.

The unit of measurement here is a **scope**, not an asset. A loading bar that names "T_Rock_02_D" is useless; one that says "Environment 12/40" is useful. A scope is a named, tagged group of load requests with a reason, optionally nested inside a parent scope, and it is what the rest of the engine gets to observe.

Two costs are kept deliberately separate:

- **Aggregate counts** are refreshed every poll from a cheap counter read on each streamable handle, so they are safe to read every frame.
- **Per-asset detail** is O(assets in scope) and runs on a slower cadence, controlled by UGantryGaugeSettings::LoadDetailPollInterval. Only pay for it when something is actually displaying asset names.

A copy of one scope's state, handed to readers.

Value type on purpose. Readers never hold the ledger's lock and never touch a live record, so a UI can poll once per frame and then take as long as it likes to render.

A consistent view of everything in flight, captured under a single lock.

Poll this once per frame. Do not hold a reference to ledger internals across frames; that is precisely the aliasing bug this type exists to prevent.

Engine subsystem that ticks the load ledger and publishes its state and events to C++ and Blueprint.

Engine scoped, so it exists before any world and survives every map change and PIE session. That matters: a loading screen has to work when there is no world at all, which rules out a world subsystem for this job.

It does not own the ledger. The ledger is owned by the GantryGauge module, which loads earlier still; this subsystem ticks it and republishes its events in a Blueprint friendly shape.

### Extending

A game subclasses this and names the subclass in DefaultGame.ini:

```cpp
[/Script/GantryGauge.GantryGaugeSettings]
StreamingSubsystemClass=/Script/MyGame.MyGameStreamingSubsystem
```

ShouldCreateSubsystem then declines for every class except the selected one, so exactly one instance exists. Without that, Unreal would create both this and the subclass.

Project-wide Gantry Gauge settings, under Project Settings -> Plugins -> Gantry Gauge.

Two kinds of entry live here and it is worth keeping them straight:

- **Class selections.** Soft class paths naming which subclass a game wants for a given hierarchy. Empty means "use the Gantry default". See GantryClassSelection.h.
- **Tunables.** Ordinary numbers and switches.

Native gameplay tags that classify load scopes by the kind of load they are.

Every one describes a *kind of load*, never a kind of gameplay. A loading screen reads these to decide what is worth showing a player without knowing anything about Gantry's internals.

Editor module that adds the live Load Gauge panel and its menu and toolbar entries.

The panel opens from the Gantry section of the level editor's Tools menu, from the Gantry button on the level editor toolbar, or from the Debug category of the developer tools menu. The same Tools menu section also offers Dump Loading State, which writes the current load ledger snapshot to the log.

Per-user preferences for Gantry Gauge's editor diagnostics.

Under Editor Preferences -> Plugins -> Gantry Gauge, saved to the user's own EditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini. Project-wide policy belongs in UGantryGaugeSettings instead.

Editor subsystem that runs Gantry Gauge's load diagnostics when a PIE session ends.

Watches PIE start and stop, which is where most Gantry diagnostics are worth running: a scope still open when PIE ends is almost always a load that never reported completion. What it does at the end of a session is set per user in UGantryGaugeEditorSettings.

Runtime UI module providing UGantryLoadingScreenWidget, a widget base that reports load ledger progress.

Widget-side companion to Gantry Gauge: a user widget base that reads the load ledger and reports named, staged progress. It deliberately does not manage a loading *screen* — surviving world teardown and the pre-engine loading phase is the engine's PreLoadScreen job, and pairing with a dedicated loading screen plugin beats reimplementing one badly.

Base widget for a Gantry loading screen, reporting progress, scope names and counts from the load ledger.

Subclass this as a Widget Blueprint and bind the events. Everything it reports comes from the ledger, so a bar built on it is showing real asset counts rather than a timer pretending to be progress.

The polling is deliberate rather than event-driven: a widget that redraws on every scope event would thrash during a large load, when frames are already scarce. Reading the streaming subsystem's snapshot every RefreshInterval seconds and easing the bar between reads is smoother and cheaper.

types.summary: Generational handle into a dense array.
types.description:
A raw index into a pooled array goes stale silently: slot 7 is freed, slot 7 is reused, and the old index now addresses a live but wrong record. Bumping a serial on free makes the stale handle detectably invalid instead. The owner of the array validates a handle by comparing its serial with the slot's current one; the handle alone can only say whether it addresses a slot at all.

Serial is signed because UHT will not expose unsigned integers to Blueprint. It only increments, and would need billions of reuse cycles on one slot to reach the sign bit.

Wired up via [/Script/Engine.Engine] AssetManagerClassName= in DefaultEngine.ini. It is created before the game instance, which makes it the earliest place the project owns.

types.summary: Root of the project's experience tree; one per project, named in Gantry Experience settings.
types.description:
### A class instead of a flag

A project has exactly one base experience, and that fact is worth more as a type than as data. UGantryExperienceSettings::BaseExperience only accepts this class, so the root cannot be mispointed; there is no Kind enum to set wrong, and "which experience is the base" has one answer enforced by the compiler and the property editor rather than by validation prose.

### What it adds structurally

Nothing. Children, stages, optional dependencies all live on the common class, because any experience can own children — the base is distinguished by being the root, not by capability. The overrides below only pin down root-ness: depth zero, no parents, no attachments.

Its Children listing doubles as the project's content registry: the base ships in chunk 0, so its entries are readable even when the content they describe is not installed. That is what lets a menu draw "Experience C — not installed" about a pak that is not there.

Any experience reachable from this base qualifies — a direct child or a deeper descendant; validation rejects anything the tree cannot reach, because an unreachable default is a boot into a guaranteed failure.

types.summary: Game feature data that stamps the plugin with build provenance for compatibility checks.
types.description:
### Plugin metadata and experience metadata

A plugin is the unit that actually ships: one cook, one pak, one set of binaries. Engine version and game version are facts about that cook, so repeating them on every experience inside the plugin would be ten copies of one truth, nine of which can drift.

An experience still carries its own metadata, because an experience in chunk 0 ships with the base game and has no plugin to inherit from. Where both exist, the plugin's is authoritative for mounting and the experience's for selection.

### Use

Set this as the GameFeatureData class for a plugin by choosing it when creating the plugin's data asset, or by pointing an existing asset's class at it. A plugin that does this takes a dependency on the Gantry plugin's GantryExperience module, which is worth entering deliberately: once plugins ship against it, Gantry cannot be lifted out of the project.

types.summary: Gantry's game feature policy, and the single place compatibility is enforced.
types.description:
### One gate

IsPluginAllowed is consulted before a plugin is mounted, and it can refuse with a reason string. Every other candidate location — the experience stage, the catalog, a menu — is downstream of a decision already taken, and putting the check there means writing it several times and having the copies disagree. One gate, consulted by everything.

### Enable it

```cpp
[/Script/GameFeatures.GameFeaturesSubsystemSettings]
GameFeaturesManagerClassName=/Script/GantryExperience.GantryGameFeaturesProjectPolicies
```

That line goes in DefaultGame.ini. Derives from UDefaultGameFeaturesProjectPolicies rather than the abstract base, so everything not overridden keeps engine-default behaviour.

types.summary: Engine subsystem that ticks the load ledger and publishes its state and events to C++ and Blueprint.
types.description:
Fired when the last user facing scope closes and the game is no longer waiting on anything. Engine subsystem that ticks the load ledger and publishes its state and events to C++ and Blueprint.

Engine scoped, so it exists before any world and survives every map change and PIE session. That matters: a loading screen has to work when there is no world at all, which rules out a world subsystem for this job.

It does not own the ledger. The ledger is owned by the GantryGauge module, which loads earlier still; this subsystem ticks it and republishes its events in a Blueprint friendly shape.

properties.name: OnScopeOpened
properties.summary: Broadcast when a load scope opens, on the thread that opened it (normally the game thread).

properties.name: OnScopeProgress
properties.summary: Broadcast on the game thread when an open scope's counts change, at most once a frame each.

properties.name: OnScopeClosed
properties.summary: Broadcast when a load scope closes, with its final state, on the thread that closed it.

properties.name: OnLoadingFinished
properties.summary: Broadcast on the game thread, on the first tick after the last user-facing scope closes.

functions.name: DumpToLog
functions.summary: Logs this frame's active and recently finished scopes.

functions.name: GetOverallProgress
functions.summary: Returns aggregate 0 to 1 progress across user facing scopes, as of this frame's snapshot.

returns.doc: Loaded over requested assets across user-facing scopes; 1 when none has requested anything.

functions.name: GetPrimaryScope
functions.summary: Returns the scope a loading bar should be naming right now.

returns.doc: The open user-facing scope with the most assets outstanding, or a default info with an invalid handle when none is open.

functions.name: GetScopeAssets
functions.summary: Copies per-asset detail for one open scope straight from the ledger, the expensive read.
functions.description: Entries exist only for handles attached while UGantryGaugeSettings::bTrackIndividualAssets was on. Each entry's bLoaded is as of the last per-asset detail refresh.

params.name: ScopeHandle
params.doc: Scope to read, e.g. FGantryLoadScopeInfo::Handle from a snapshot.

params.name: OutAssets
params.doc: Receives the scope's tracked assets; emptied when the handle is stale.

returns.doc: False when the scope has closed, the handle is stale or the ledger is unavailable.

functions.name: GetSnapshot
functions.summary: Returns a consistent view of everything in flight, as captured on this frame's tick.
functions.description: Captured once per frame whether or not anyone asks, so any number of widgets can read it for free. Empty until the subsystem has ticked once.

returns.doc: The cached snapshot, valid until the next tick replaces it.

functions.name: IsLoading
functions.summary: Returns true while any user facing scope is in flight, as of this frame's snapshot.

returns.doc: True when the cached snapshot has an open user-facing scope.

members.name: ShouldCreateSubsystem
members.summary: Declines unless this class is the one UGantryGaugeSettings::StreamingSubsystemClass selects, or the Gantry default when that setting is empty, so exactly one instance exists.

members.name: Initialize
members.summary: Subscribes to the ledger's events and starts a core ticker that runs with or without a world.

members.name: Deinitialize
members.summary: Removes the ticker and unsubscribes from the ledger.

members.name: Get
members.summary: Returns the engine's streaming subsystem, or null before engine init and after shutdown.
